outline.chapter_title: 1. Factual Background, Statutory Claims, and the Case’s Unusual Procedural Posture
outline.description: This chapter introduces the employment relationship, the challenged overtime policy change, the Minnesota statutory claims Cohen asserted, and the procedural developments that shaped the appeal. It explains why the case became focused less on unpaid wages themselves and more on penalties, jurisdiction, and available remedies after Consilio paid the claimed overtime and liquidated damages.
subtopics: Consilio’s business and Cohen’s role as a Minnesota-based hourly licensed attorney document reviewer
The July 2019 email announcing the new overtime policy and the elimination of premium overtime pay
Cohen’s 2020 lawsuit on behalf of himself and a putative class
The three Minnesota statutory theories: MPWA, MFLSA, and MWTA
Requested remedies: overtime wages, liquidated damages, statutory penalties, and injunctive relief
Consilio’s payment of overtime wages and MFLSA liquidated damages to Cohen and similarly situated employees
The parties’ stipulations that Cohen had been paid all overtime wages and MFLSA liquidated damages he claimed
Why the remaining dispute centered on statutory penalties and other non-wage remedies
The parties’ agreement to resolve the case through summary judgment before further discovery
The district court’s complete grant of summary judgment and the issues presented on appeal

outline.chapter_title: 2. Appellate Framework and the Minnesota Payment of Wages Act Claim
outline.description: This chapter explains the Eighth Circuit’s standard of review and then closely examines the MPWA issue: whether an employee may personally recover average daily wage penalties under Minn. Stat. §§ 181.171 and 181.101. It traces the court’s textual analysis and shows how the opinion distinguishes between employee wage claims and commissioner-enforced penalties.
subtopics: De novo review of summary judgment and the no-genuine-issue standard
How the court frames the MPWA question as one of statutory authorization for penalties
Section 181.171’s private right of action for specified MPWA violations
The significance of § 181.171’s language limiting civil penalties or damages to those 'provided for in the section violated'
Cohen’s argument that § 181.101 plainly authorizes average daily wage penalties
The court’s reading of § 181.101(a) as assigning penalty enforcement to the Commissioner
The statutory sequence: commissioner demand, ten-day nonpayment period, then commissioner collection of wages and penalties
The distinction between money paid over to the employee and authority to seek the penalty in the first place
The employee’s preserved right under § 181.101 to prosecute a claim for wages, but not necessarily for statutory penalties
Use of Minnesota interpretive principles, including plain-language analysis
The court’s comparison to §§ 181.13 and 181.14, where the legislature expressly gave employees authority to collect penalties
The 'legislature knows how' inference and its role in the court’s reasoning
Supporting authority from Minnesota and federal cases, including Allan, Milner, Lagasse, and Hull
The holding that only the Commissioner may seek § 181.101 average daily wage penalties, and affirmance on the MPWA claim

outline.chapter_title: 3. The MFLSA Claim: Paid Wages, Remaining Penalties, and Article III Jurisdiction
outline.description: This chapter focuses on the opinion’s most important procedural move: vacating and remanding the MFLSA ruling because of unresolved federal jurisdictional concerns. It explains how the case shifted from merits to standing and mootness once Cohen was fully paid for overtime and liquidated damages, and how the court relied on federal justiciability principles to require further examination in the district court.
subtopics: Cohen’s stipulation that he had received all overtime wages and liquidated damages allegedly due under the MFLSA
The remaining MFLSA dispute over statutory penalties payable to the Commissioner rather than directly to Cohen
Why a plaintiff must have standing for each claim and each form of requested relief
The relationship between standing at the outset and mootness as the case continues
Friends of the Earth v. Laidlaw and the idea that civil penalties can sometimes redress injury through deterrence of ongoing or future violations
Town of Chester and the requirement of relief-specific standing
Sisney and the continuity principle linking standing and mootness
Voluntary cessation doctrine and why a defendant’s change in conduct does not automatically moot a case
The key factual uncertainty identified by the Eighth Circuit: whether Consilio’s challenged overtime policy remains in effect
How continued existence of the policy could preserve a live claim for civil penalties under a deterrence theory
How discontinuation of the policy, coupled with no reasonable expectation of recurrence, could render the MFLSA claim moot
Why the appellate court declined to decide the jurisdictional issue on the existing record
The remedy: vacatur of summary judgment on the MFLSA claim and remand for the district court to determine its jurisdiction
The special concurrence’s caution about whether Laidlaw standing applies here at all, and its additional note regarding fees, costs, and prejudgment interest

outline.chapter_title: 4. The MWTA Notice Claim and the Limits of Appellate Argument
outline.description: This chapter examines Cohen’s claim under the Minnesota Wage Theft Act based on allegedly inadequate notice of the overtime-policy change. It shows that the court did not resolve a broad substantive question about the MWTA, but instead affirmed because Cohen failed to identify a statutory basis for penalties and failed to present meaningful appellate argument.
subtopics: The nature of the MWTA allegation: failure to provide required notice of a change in employment terms under § 181.032
Cohen’s theory that the 2019 overtime-policy communication violated the statute
The practical effect of Cohen’s stipulation that he had already received all compensation owed
The court’s focus on the absence of identified statutory authority authorizing civil penalties for this claim
The appellate court’s response to Cohen’s complaint that the district court gave little attention to the claim
Waiver and forfeiture through inadequate briefing on appeal
Use of Milligan v. City of Red Oak to support refusal to consider unsupported arguments
Why the court affirmed dismissal of the MWTA claim without extensive merits analysis

outline.chapter_title: 5. Injunctive Relief, Pleading Discipline, and the Final Disposition
outline.description: This chapter ties together the remedial issues outside the wage-and-penalty statutes, especially Cohen’s request for injunctive relief. It explains why the court refused to consider a newly reframed injunction request, then concludes with the opinion’s final disposition and what remains for the district court on remand.
subtopics: Cohen’s appellate argument for an injunction requiring Consilio to rescind the overtime policy
The difference between the injunctive relief requested in the complaint and the revised relief requested later in summary judgment briefing
The rule that new claims or materially different requests for relief must be raised through amendment, not motion briefing
Reliance on InfoDeli and Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 15(a)
Why the district court did not err by not addressing the newly framed injunction request
The appellate disposition: affirmance in part, vacatur in part, and remand
What was affirmed: the MPWA ruling, the MWTA ruling, and rejection of the injunction argument as presented
What was vacated: the MFLSA summary judgment ruling because of unresolved jurisdictional questions
What the district court must address on remand: standing, mootness, and any consequences for remaining relief and possible fees-related issues noted by the concurrence
The case’s broader significance as an example of how payment of merits relief can transform a wage-and-hour case into a remedies and justiciability dispute
